analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour and ends lower wage floors for tipped, teen, and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Raise the Wage Act 231-199 on July 18, 2019, but the Senate placed it on its calendar and never voted, and it died at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps over seven years, from the $7.25 floor to $15 an hour, and then index it to the growth in the median wage so it keeps rising automatically. It would also phase out the separate lower minimum wages for tipped workers, newly hired workers under 20, and workers with disabilities, so everyone would be covered by one wage floor. The House passed it, but the Senate never brought it to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning the federal minimum wage or just above it, including tipped restaurant workers whose employers may pay as little as $2.13 an hour in cash, and workers with disabilities paid under special subminimum-wage certificates. Roughly 20-30 million workers were projected to see raises, since a higher wage floor also lifts pay for people earning somewhat above the minimum.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in annual steps — $8.40, $9.50, $10.60, $11.70, $12.80, $13.90, $15.00 — over seven years [S5].
After reaching $15, the wage is indexed to the annual percentage increase in the median hourly wage of all employees, so it rises automatically instead of staying fixed for years [S5].
Phases out the tipped minimum wage, which lets restaurants pay tipped workers a far lower cash wage, so those workers would be guaranteed the full minimum wage [S2, S5].

Phases out the special subminimum-wage certificates that allow employers to pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage, with Labor Department transition assistance and a GAO report on business impact [S4, S5].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay the federal minimum wage or the tipped and subminimum wages — concentrated in restaurants, hotels, retail, agriculture, and other low-wage industries — would face higher payroll costs. Small businesses with thin margins would bear this alongside large chains. Consumers could see modest price increases where labor costs are passed through.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers like restaurants and retailers

drawbacks.text: A sharply higher federal wage floor applies everywhere, including low-cost rural areas where $15 exceeds the local prevailing wage; critics argued this would reduce hours, speed automation, or cut jobs in some places [S8].

The bill requires a GAO report on the first wage increases' effects on businesses and lets Congress recommend delaying later increases based on the findings, an acknowledgment by the bill's own drafters that the schedule might need adjustment [S5].

Ending the subminimum wage for workers with disabilities could risk some sheltered-workshop jobs even as it guarantees equal pay; the bill includes transition assistance precisely because of that concern [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are large and concrete: a seven-year path from $7.25 to $15 with automatic indexing, and an end to legal subminimum pay for tipped and disabled workers. The real cost is to low-wage employers' payroll, and the strongest honest objection is that a uniform national floor can bite harder in low-wage regions; the bill's built-in GAO reporting and Congressional review of later increases is a partial answer but does not adjust the floor itself. On balance the benefit to the tens of millions of workers at or near the minimum outweighs the diffuse cost spread across employers and prices.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 231-199, but the Senate put it on its calendar and never scheduled a vote, so it died when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Education and Labor Committee marked up the bill and reported it by a vote of 28-20 on March 6, 2019 [S7].
The House passed the bill on July 18, 2019, by a recorded vote of 231-199; Democrats voted 228-6 in favor while Republicans voted 3-192 against [S8, S7].
A Republican motion to recommit, which would have exempted businesses with fewer than 10 employees and under $1 million in sales, failed 210-218 [S8, S7].
The Senate received the bill and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders on July 22, 2019; no further Senate action followed for the rest of the Congress [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay at or near the federal minimum wage — restaurants, hotels, retail, and agriculture — are better off, since the higher wage floor never took effect. The 205 House cosponsors and the 231 members who voted yes got a floor vote but no law.

sides.party_line_note: All 205 cosponsors were Democrats [S6]. The House passed it 231-199 with Democrats voting 228-6 for and Republicans 3-192 against; the one Independent voting also voted no [S8].

industries.note: The largest group of minimum-wage employers; the bill would end the tipped minimum wage that lets them pay servers as little as $2.13 in cash, directly raising their payroll costs in exchange for higher pay for millions of workers.

industries.industry: Hotels, retail, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: Large low-wage employers would face higher wage floors over seven years, with costs passed to consumers or absorbed in margins.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and employers holding 14(c) subminimum certificates
industries.note: The bill bars new special certificates and sunsets existing ones, ending the legal ability to pay workers with disabilities below the minimum wage.

Small businesses paying above $15 would see little change; those paying the minimum would face the same cost increase as large chains, with no blanket exemption — a Republican amendment to exempt firms with fewer than 10 employees and under $1 million in sales was defeated 210-218.
